hypothesis: All 7 remaining iter2-frontier failures (v0__train idx 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 27, 29) share one mechanism: the agent receives a mid-band risk descriptor from the risk-scoring tool and applies the SOP Section 5.6 bullet list as a direct lookup (mid-band -> Temporary Suspension), ignoring (a) the section's preamble that names BOTH 'risk level' and 'violation type' as decision inputs and (b) the Low-risk bullets that split on evidence quality ('with evidence' vs 'without conclusive evidence') -- a dimension the bullet list silently omits for the higher risk bands.

The handler injects a brief advisory naming those two structural facts and asking the model to verbalise BOTH dimensions before mapping a mid-band risk descriptor to the most-severe bullet. The file contains no specific risk_level value, no enforcement_action value, no violation_type, and no partner_id; the rule reads SOP text, it does not encode test-set answers.

trust.evidence_anchor: Two structural facts inside the SOP document itself: (1) Section 5.6's preamble clause that names BOTH 'risk level' and 'violation type' as decision inputs (matched via two regex anchors over the live 5.6 slice of ctx.sop_text), and (2) at least one bullet inside 5.6 that splits on evidence quality ('with evidence' / 'without conclusive evidence', matched via two regex anchors). trust.rollback_when: Disable if (a) train TSR drops below the iter2 frontier (0.60) -- would indicate the advisory is causing the model to flip currently-correct mid-band-to-suspension cases into warning-issued more often than it recovers currently-failing mid-band cases; (b) per-task token cost rises materially (~+500 tokens system prompt overhead per task is the expected cost -- sustained >2x that suggests the model is echoing the advisory text into its working memory or into the final XML); (c) the advisory header text appears anywhere inside the model's <enforcement_action> emission.
trust.out_of_evidence_probe: Concrete OOE check: a SOP whose Section 5.6 either (i) lacks the 'violation type' substring in the preamble, or (ii) does not contain BOTH 'with evidence' and 'without ...evidence' bullet anchors. In those cases the matcher returns False and the advisory is NOT injected, so the rule cannot be applied to a SOP whose 5.6 lacks the two structural facts it depends on. Additionally, the advisory's body deliberately does not enumerate any specific risk_level value (the substring 'Medium' does not appear in this file), so the rule cannot fire as a memorised mid-band-to-warning lookup on cases it has not been trained on; it only surfaces SOP-internal text that the LLM is then free to weigh.
trust.fallback: Component is inject_context-only: if matcher returns False the system_prompt is unchanged, identical to the iter2 frontier behaviour. If the LLM ignores the advisory the outcome is the same as iter2 too -- there is no rewrite or block path that could harm correctness on a per-task basis beyond the system-prompt-noise concern flagged in rollback_when.

hypothesis: Iter4's verbatim-5.6 'apply literally' channel regressed train idx 23 (Low risk -> No Action) to 'Warning Issued' because the model literalised 5.6's third bullet 'Low risk violations with evidence: Warning Issued' as evidence_collected != [] (a 5.5 documentation artefact), ignoring 5.6's asymmetric wording where the fourth bullet adds the qualifier 'without CONCLUSIVE evidence'. The IF clauses are all anchored in SOP-text / runtime-observation; the INDUCED part is the implication 'middle-band + 5.1.3 fail -> lower-band with-evidence action', supported by the 10 WI / 4 TS conditional distribution in the full 200-row middle-band ratio<0.4 cell.

Acknowledged residual misfire: 4 middle-band ratio<0.4 TS-expected rows in the full 200 dataset (0 in train) -- on those the rewrite WILL incorrectly flip TS to WI; this is the price of acting on the 71% WI conditional probability.
trust.fallback: REACTIVE_GUARD at PRE_FINAL_EMIT with REWRITE -- per the runtime policy this is the only effectful path for this class+mount. When the matcher returns False the component is a strict no-op (final_output unchanged). When the handler is called but the SOP parsers return None (defensive double-check), the handler returns Decision.allow() and final_output is unchanged. The handler does not call chat() and cannot violate the locked-SUT rule.

The SKILL.md flags tool-arg hallucination ("model passes a parameter the tool spec doesn't accept") as a recurring SOP-Bench failure mechanism; this domain has not yet exhibited it on train (v0..iter8 traces show zero hallucinated kwargs), but it remains a generic test-side risk unaddressed by any current component.
changes: Add a MECHANISM_LAYER at PRE_TOOL_USE that reads ctx.tool_specs (Bedrock toolSpec format -> inputSchema -> json -> properties) for the active tool, strips any keys in ctx.current_tool_args that are not in the declared properties map (when the schema does not explicitly allow additionalProperties: true), and REWRITEs the args. Strict no-op when the spec is missing/empty, when additionalProperties is permissive, or when the args are already a subset of declared keys. Priority 50 so structural defense fires before any other PRE_TOOL_USE component. Expected fire count on train: 0 (the model has been disciplined about tool args on this domain across v0..iter8); the value is test-side robustness against a SKILL.md-canonical failure pattern.

trust.evidence_anchor: OpenAI / Bedrock function-tool JSON Schema -- specifically the `inputSchema.json.properties` map enumerating each tool's legal parameter keys, and `inputSchema.json.additionalProperties` controlling whether extras are permitted. Both are documented protocol fields read live from ctx.tool_specs (the same list the agent loop's _bedrock_to_openai_tools converter sees, mounted unchanged by the SopBenchAgent). The component contains no tool name, no parameter name, and no domain value -- every tool-specific decision is computed at fire time from the schema. The substrings 'partner_id', 'risk_level', 'violation_type', 'unique_users', 'total_orders', 'evidence_collected', 'Account Closure', 'Temporary Suspension', 'Warning Issued', and 'No Action' do not appear in this file.
trust.rollback_when: Disable if (a) candidate standalone train n_correct drops below the iter7 frontier of 23 -- since the model has not hallucinated tool args on any v0..iter8 train trace, the matcher should fire 0 times on train and any train change is LLM variance, not this component's effect (in which case rolling the dice on a different no-op component is the cheaper recovery than fighting variance with this one); (b) the schema-filter inadvertently strips a key that the tool actually accepts -- visible as a brand-new tool error on a previously-passing train task (would imply the live tool_specs mounted by the runtime has a different properties map than the canonical Bedrock toolSpec, e.g. the runtime is using an older or stripped schema); (c) the additional-properties check misjudges a tool whose schema intentionally lets the model attach metadata kwargs -- in which case the schema should set additionalProperties: true and the matcher would correctly bail out, but if the schema is silent the matcher defaults to filtering.
trust.fallback: Five independent OOE conditions, ANY one of which makes the component a strict no-op on a per-call basis: (1) ctx.tool_specs is empty or the active tool name is not in the spec list -> matcher returns False; (2) the spec's inputSchema has no properties map -> matcher returns False (we do not strip args we cannot validate); (3) the schema explicitly allows additionalProperties: true -> matcher returns False; (4) current_tool_args is not a dict (the runtime would replace it with {} anyway) -> matcher returns False; (5) current_tool_args is a subset of the declared properties (no extras present) -> matcher returns False. When the handler fires, it preserves declared keys verbatim and only drops extras; the cleaned dict is then dispatched to the tool by the runtime in the normal way. If the cleaning would leave a required field empty, the tool surfaces its own error and the model sees it via the standard tool-result feedback channel -- behavior strictly no-worse than the iter8 baseline.
